country.name: Iraq
country.tagline: Mesopotamia's beer country, where wine was the imported luxury of kings.

stats.note: No significant modern wine production; Christian villages in the north make small amounts.

country.overview:
In ancient Mesopotamia beer was the everyday drink and wine an expensive import. The alluvial plains of Sumer and Babylonia were too hot, flat and salty for good vines, so wine came down the Tigris and Euphrates from the hills of the north and from Syria and the Zagros; Sumerian texts call it the beer of the mountains. The trade route that ran past Godin Tepe in the Zagros carried wine to the lowland cities by the late fourth millennium BC.

Royal archives show wine as a palace luxury. At Mari on the Euphrates, letters of the eighteenth century BC discuss wine shipments; at Nimrud (Kalhu), the Assyrian capital, the so-called wine lists of the eighth century BC record rations for the royal household and staff; and a famous relief from Nineveh shows King Ashurbanipal and his queen drinking wine beneath a grapevine, with the severed head of an enemy king hanging nearby. The hills of northern Iraq, in today's Kurdistan region, had vineyards in Assyrian times.

Today Iraq has no notable wine industry. Assyrian and Chaldean Christian villages around Alqosh and in the Nineveh plains make small amounts of wine and arak for church and home.

country.climate_soils: Hot alluvial plains; vines only in the northern hills.

sites.name: Nimrud (Kalhu)
sites.text: The Assyrian capital Kalhu on the Tigris, whose 'wine lists' of the eighth century BC record wine rations issued to the royal household and palace staff. In Mesopotamia wine was a costly import from the northern hills.

sites.name: Nineveh
sites.text: Assyrian capital whose relief of Ashurbanipal's banquet shows the king drinking wine beneath a vine.
